scenes.title: Change the start, keep the stride.
A contiguous view can share storage.
New offsets belong to new storage.

cues.text: Chapter Five follows the selected values into storage. An element offset counts values from the start of that storage, beginning at zero.
Our five by five FP32 tensor stores one row after another: row-major order. Each value uses four bytes. Large labels show values; small labels show element offsets.
Selecting row zero makes a view into the original storage. Its five values occupy consecutive element offsets. Making this view copies no values.
Stride is the distance, in elements, between successive selected values. Here stride one means four bytes. A byte offset measures distance in bytes from the storage's start.
Column zero uses offsets zero, five, ten, fifteen and twenty. The next selected value is five element positions away, so this view has stride five.
Five FP32 elements span twenty bytes, so its byte stride is twenty. The highlighted values stay in the original storage; selecting the column has not moved them together.
Choose column one instead. Its first selected value begins one element into the same storage. The starting offset changes, but the stride remains five.
Changing the column index still gives a view. To put the selected values next to one another, we need a different layout in separate storage.
Calling contiguous on this column creates a packed copy: a new buffer with the same selected values in consecutive positions. The original storage is unchanged.
The copy has stride one and new element offsets zero through four. Five four-byte values mean twenty bytes of values copied; copying also reads and writes memory.
A row already has consecutive values. In row one, they begin at offset five and have stride one. Calling contiguous can return this row without copying.
Contiguous describes the order of the values. A contiguous view can share another tensor's storage and start at a non-zero offset; it need not own a separate buffer.
Now take column three and make a packed copy. Predict the new copy's element offsets and stride. Do its offsets keep the original column's starting position?
How many bytes of values are copied, and does the original tensor change? Use the four-byte value size, then pause and explain before checking.
The new buffer starts at its own offset zero. Its five element offsets are zero through four, with stride one. Twenty bytes of values are copied.
The original tensor, selected values and multiplication results are unchanged. Return to Chapter Five and compare a view with a packed copy, separating layout, copy cost and measured performance.
